data.title: Pavol Satko: Constantine Porphyrogenitus and his Moravias
data.excerpt: Articles often claim that the name Great Moravia is very old and that the Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (944–959) had already used it in De administrando imperio. Pavol Satko reads that work closely and argues that its “megale Moravia” lay between the Upper Tisza and Transylvania, where the Hungarian tribal federation lived in the emperor’s day — not in the realm of the Mojmirids.
data.metaDescription: Pavol Satko examines what “megale Moravia” really means in De administrando imperio, the handbook of the Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus.

children.text: Many articles will tell you that the name Great Moravia, used today, is very old and that it was employed long ago by the Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, who reigned from 944 to 959. His work De administrando imperio (hereafter “the DAI”) contains the phrase “megale Moravia”, and it is a regular source of controversy when the extent and location of the Mojmirid dominions in the 9th century are being determined. Often simply because nobody reads the DAI properly, nobody knows anything about how it came into being, and so they join together what cannot be joined. Let us look at what Constantine actually wrote about “megale Moravia”, and in what circumstances. Besides the DAI, his other work De Ceremoniis aule byzantine (hereafter “the Ceremoniis”) and the works of the Byzantine historians of the day are also of marginal interest for the description of Great Moravia. It is time to start another debate, so let us begin with quotations:
Quotations from De administrando imperio (DAI)
In the DAI, chapter 13, Of the nations that are neighbours to the Turks:

blocks.text: In the neighbourhood of the Turks dwell these nations: on their western side is the land of the Franks, to the north dwell the Pechenegs, and on the southern side is great Moravia, that is, the country of Svatopluk, which these Turks have utterly laid waste and taken for themselves. On the side of the mountains the Croats are neighbours to the Turks.
blocks.author: Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus
blocks.source: De administrando imperio, ch. 13 – Of the nations that are neighbours to the Turks

children.text: In the DAI, chapter 38, Of the genealogy of the nation of the Turks, and whence they are descended:

blocks.text: After some time the Pechenegs attacked the Turks and drove them out together with their prince Árpád. The Turks turned to flight and sought a land in which they might settle. Thus they came, drove out the people inhabiting great Moravia, settled in their country and dwell there to this day. From that time the Turks have never again met the Pechenegs in battle.
blocks.author: Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus
blocks.source: De administrando imperio, ch. 38 – Of the genealogy of the nation of the Turks

children.text: In the DAI, chapter 40, Of the clans of the Kabars and the Turks

blocks.text: ...the Turks, after being driven out by the Pechenegs, settled in the land in which they are today. In that place there are landmarks from days of old. The first is the bridge of the emperor Trajan, standing at the beginning of the country of the Turks. Three days’ journey from this bridge is Belgrade, with the tower of the holy and great emperor Constantine. On the way back, at the bend of the river, two days’ journey from Belgrade, is the so-called Sirmium. Beyond these places stretches great Moravia, the unbaptised, which the Turks destroyed and over which Svatopluk ruled in former days. These, then, are the notable points along the river Danube and their names. The territories lying higher up, however, which are settled by the Turks, are at present named after the rivers that flow through them. These rivers are as follows: the first of them is the Temes, the second the river Tutis, the third the river Maroš, the fourth the river Kriš and yet another the river Tisa. The neighbours of the Turks are, on the eastern side, the Bulgarians, from whom they are separated by the river Istros, also called the Danube, to the north the Pechenegs, to the west the Franks and to the south the Croats.” and also “It must be known that Teveli died and that it was his son Termaču who came recently (to us) as a friend together with Bulču, the third prince and karchas of Turkey
blocks.author: Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus
blocks.source: De administrando imperio, ch. 40 – Of the clans of the Kabars and the Turks

children.text: In the DAI, chapter 41, Of the country of Moravia

blocks.text:
It must be known that Svatopluk, the ruler of Moravia, was a brave man and feared among the nations that bordered on him. This Svatopluk had three sons. As he lay dying, he divided his country into three parts and left one part to each of his sons. The first he solemnly appointed great ruler, on the condition that the two remaining sons should be subject to the sovereignty of the first son. He then admonished them not to fall into discord and not to set themselves one against another. He showed them the following example: he brought three rods and bound them together; he gave them to the first son to break them; when his strength was not enough for that, he handed them again to the second and in the same way to the third as well; then he separated the three rods and handed them to his sons one by one; they took them and, at his bidding that they should break them, they did so. By this example he admonished them and said: If you live in concord and love, you will become indivisible, your enemies will not overcome you and will not defeat you. But if strife and rivalry arise among you and you divide the country into three separate dominions not subject to the first brother, you will destroy one another and the neighbouring enemies too will destroy you utterly.
After Svatopluk’s death the brothers managed to live in peace for a year. Then, however, strife and quarrels arose among them and they began to fight one another. At that point the Turks came and destroyed them utterly, seized their country and inhabit it to this day. And those who survived scattered and fled to the neighbouring tribes, to the Bulgarians, the Turks, the Croats and the other nations.
blocks.author: Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus
blocks.source: De administrando imperio, ch. 41 – Of the country of Moravia

children.text: In the DAI, chapter 42, A description of the lands from Thessalonica to the river Danube and to the city of Belgrade, a description of Turkey and of the country of the Pechenegs as far as the Khazar city of Sarkel, and of Russia.

blocks.text: It must be known that from Thessalonica to the river Danube, where the city called Belgrade lies, is eight days’ journey, if, however, a man does not travel quickly but with halts. The Turks dwell beyond the river Danube in the territory of Moravia, but also on this side of the river, between the Danube and the river Sava.
blocks.author: Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus

children.text: A quotation from De Ceremoniis aule byzantine (the Ceremoniis)
In the Ceremoniis, book II, chapter 48.

blocks.text: To the rulers of the Turks a letter with a golden seal and the address: A letter of the emperor of Constantinople and of the Romans who love Christ, to the princes of Turkey. The same inscription and the same seal also for the letter to the princes of the Pechenegs. For the prince of Croatia, Serbia, Dioclea, Moravia, Terbounia, Kanale and Zachlumia a letter with the address: A commission of the Christ-loving emperor for the ruler of the province ... with a golden seal.
blocks.author: Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus
blocks.source: De Ceremoniis aulae byzantinae, book II, ch. 48

children.text: So much for the quotations; now let us go through some of the realities of that time connected with this part of the DAI, because the correct understanding of the text proceeds from them.
Why Constantine wrote “Turks”.

Right at the outset we should explain why Constantine — and after him, for several centuries, other Byzantine chroniclers and rulers as well — used the name Turks for the people we today call the “Old Hungarians”, and whom the West of the day, including the ancestors of today’s Slovaks, named the Ugri.

The Turks come from the territory beyond what is today northern China, from which they spread across Central Asia and part of south-eastern Europe. The Byzantines encountered the Turks as early as 568, and in 627 the Turks helped the emperor Heraclius to victory over the Persians. For four hundred years they had known the Turks, and in the 10th century the elite of the “Old Hungarians” not only seemed to them to be Turks in their way of life, dress and warfare, but a part of that elite certainly was Turkic. This “Turkic” elite lived at that time, in the 7th century, south of the river Kama together with a Finno-Ugric population that came from the southern forest belt on the western side of the Urals. We cannot determine exactly when the Finno-Ugrians were subjugated by the Turks, but it may have happened only after the Turkic invasion of the southern Russian steppes around the year 559, in the course of which they drove the Avars into the Carpathian Basin. This was also the view of Herman Wamberger, or Ármin Vámbéry, a native of Svätý Jur.

The Byzantines clearly distinguished between Finno-Ugric and Turkic ethnicity and, although they knew the designation Ungri, in those times they used it only rarely. The name Ugri, Onoguri, Ungri expresses something like a tribal alliance, and it was spread to the West by the Slavs — either merchants who travelled down the Volga to Persia, or the people of Kyiv, who, like the Ugri, were for a time vassals of the powerful western Göktürks, the Khazars.
Who in fact were the “Turks” in Constantine’s time.

But there was a difference between the “Turks” whom the Byzantines came to know in the days of the emperor Heraclius and the “Turks” Constantine writes about. By then the Finno-Ugric and Turkic tribes also included the three tribes of the Kabars, who were the first to penetrate into the Carpathian Basin and who, at the time the DAI was written, lived on the Upper Tisza according to some historians. The prevailing view is that the Kabars were originally Khazars of the Jewish faith who came into a power struggle with the supreme ruler of the Khazars, the khagan. There is, however, another view, held above all among Muslim historians, according to which the Kabars were Mohammedans who did not accept the “state” Jewish religion of the Khazars, and their flight to the West had a religious reason.

But the problem with the composition of the population recorded in the DAI under the name “Turks” does not end with the Kabars. Persian and Chinese historians used the designation Bashkir. Some understand all the Ugri under that name, others only those Ugri who are Mohammedans, and still others use it for a distinct group of Turkic origin from Central Asia which lived as guests alongside the “Old Hungarians”. Since we are on the word Magyars, the closest to the name we use today is the Arabic designation Magyars (al-Maggarija) from the year 870, when the “Turks” still lived north of the Black Sea.

And finally we must not forget that the elite designated as “Turks” in the year 950 included not only people who came from the east into the Carpathian Basin around the year 900, but also a part of the elite of the original population, which submitted and became vassals or entered into an alliance. This is attested by the Slavic names of the commanders who led the raids of the “Old Hungarians” to the west. We shall therefore not use the name “Turks” or “Old Hungarians”, but a broader one, one of those used by Hungarian historians in their English-language papers. There are three to choose from: Levedis Tribal Alliance, Hungarian Tribal Alliance or Hungarian Tribal Federation. These multi-word names correspond to different periods and also to different degrees of political and military centralisation. For the year 950 the last of them suits best, because a federation presupposes the existence of a chief representative, even if often with limited authority. This excellent name was used by Sándor László Tóth, and it best reflects the situation in which, during the second half of the 10th century, the Árpád clan became the leading family clan in the Carpathian Basin. A slavish translation of the name into Slovak as Maďarský kmeňový zväz is, for the reasons given above, unsuitable, and so from here on we shall use only the abbreviation HTF for Constantine’s “Turks”.

children.text: A little order among the names Moravia.

The problem of correctly interpreting the DAI, and the Ceremoniis as well, rests on the name Moravia, which has various geographical, political and historical meanings. So that we do not have to describe at length and precisely each time which Moravia we have in mind, we must put the “Moravias” in order with the help of distinguishing names:
- The Moravia mentioned in the Ceremoniis, that is the country in Serbia on the river Velika Morava, which flows into the Danube from the right side before the Iron Gates, we shall call “
Provincia Moravia

- The Moravia where the core of the Mojmirid dominions lay, i.e. the country on both banks of the river Morava, which flows into the Danube from the left side below Devín, i.e. the territory from today’s Olomouc to Devín, we shall call “
Lower Moravia
- The territory of the empire ruled by the Mojmirids, especially during the reign of Svatopluk I, we shall call by the modern name “
Great Moravia
- The Moravia as the emperor Constantine understood it, where the HTF lived, we shall call “
megale Moravia
How the DAI and the Ceremoniis came into being

According to the generally accepted view, Constantine wrote the DAI between the years 949 and 952, and the Ceremoniis in 956 to 959. Both works were created for practical life. The Ceremoniis was to serve to preserve the traditions that strengthened imperial rule and the Byzantine empire, and the DAI came into being as a practical handbook for the policy of Constantine’s successor Romanos II (938–963). Let us assess what was written, but in the reverse order to the one in which the records came into being. First the Ceremoniis and then the DAI.
The record in the Ceremoniis

In the extensive work the Ceremoniis there is a part dealing with imperial correspondence. In those days, even if sometimes in hostile times, a cultivated form of mutual correspondence existed between rulers. The manner of the opening address, the use of the correct title and the quality of the attached seals really mattered, and even an unintended lapse could be understood as disrespect and give cause for war. Byzantium conducted a lively correspondence from England to India and, besides secular rulers, it also communicated intensively with church figures. Constantine created a set of rules, in which he drew on the long-standing diplomatic practices of the imperial administration. It may be assumed that something like a reference manual consisting of a mass of notes and correspondence existed in the palace, and that Constantine made an updated administrative regulation out of them.

The Ceremoniis contains the contemporary titles of the rulers of the countries with which Byzantium then corresponded, and the address of the addressee also takes account of their mutual position of power. Chapter 48 is a list of countries and dignitaries around the year 950. “Great Moravia”, which had not existed for 50 years, is not mentioned in it, because Constantine knew of its demise. Unfortunately the emperor did not even mention whether correspondence with the Mojmirids had existed at some time in the past, and so in this area the only sources are the Lives of the two apostles of the Slavs, whose evidential value is not absolute.

blocks.caption: The emperor Michael III (the one who received the embassy from Rastislav) receiving the “post”. Source: The Illustrated Chronicle of Ioannes Skylitzes in Madrid
blocks.alt: The emperor Michael III (the one who received the embassy from Rastislav) receiving the “post”. Source: The Illustrated Chronicle of Ioannes Skylitzes in Madrid

children.text: As can be seen from the quotation, in the Ceremoniis the emperor writes about the princes of the HTF. It follows from the form of address that the princes of the HTF were not dependent on Byzantium. What is even more interesting, from Byzantium’s point of view the individual princes are independent and are not subject to the central power of the Árpád grand prince, because no other, higher form of correspondence directly with the Árpáds exists (a different address, more golden seals).

In the same chapter a country by the name of Moravia is written about together with countries such as Croatia, Serbia, Dioclea and others in Dalmatia and Illyria. From the address of its ruler a certain subordination follows, even if only a formal one, and it is therefore evident that this is not “Great Moravia”. The order of the countries in this part of the work creates a certain geographical connection. Together with the form of address, that defines the Moravia mentioned there as the region on the river Velika Morava in central Serbia and south of the Danube. This conclusion is also confirmed by a record from the year 975, which documents that Adralestos Diogenes was the strategos of Moravia. It is evident that nobody of such a name and title lived at that time in “our” Moravia. The Ceremoniis unambiguously records the “province of Moravia”.
The source of Constantine’s information

When you read the records in the DAI carefully, it is striking how relatively small the territory in which the HTF resided was, as the emperor defined it by rivers. He recorded the names of the rivers in the Tisza basin, but does not mention the Váh and the Hron above the Danube, nor the rivers Leitha or Rába in Transdanubia. What is still more surprising is that for the seats of the HTF he does not use the older Roman geographical designations such as Pannonia I, Pannonia Valeria, Pannonia II or Savia, and above all that he did not use the names Sarmatia or Dacia. There may be two reasons for this geographically limited form of record. Either the HTF really did live only in the territory mentioned in the year 950, or the reason is the source of information that was used — and perhaps both.

In the year 943 the conflict between Byzantium and the HTF was ended by a five-year peace agreement. Many prominent members of the HTF then fell into Byzantine captivity and became hostages. In the DAI, in chapter 40, the emperor writes about the visit of Termaču and Bulču, which took place in the year 948 and was probably taken up with peace talks. Two more visits followed this one up to the year 952.

First a repeated visit by Bulču, during which Bulču had himself baptised, was honoured with the title of patrikios and received a large sum of money. The historian Skylitzes recorded that after his return from Constantinople Bulču renounced Christianity, and that divine punishment therefore overtook him. After the battle lost on the river Lech in the year 955, Bulču was hanged in Regensburg.

The third visit was made by the archon (prince) Gylas - Gyula, who also had himself baptised, also received the title of patrikios and certainly the appropriate sum of money as well. But Gylas, unlike Bulču, remained a believing Christian and left Constantinople together with the monk Hierotheos, who had been appointed bishop of the “Turks” by the patriarch of Constantinople. Gyula is probably not a name but rather a title, and the prince’s personal “pagan” name was, according to the historian György Györffy, Zombor. Zombor was baptised in Constantinople with the name Stephen. The choice of name was not accidental at all. Stephen is the name of the first martyr of Christianity, and in the Christianisation of new gentes it was customary to baptise the supreme ruler of the pagans with this name. Just as Gyula was in Constantinople, so the Árpád grand prince Géza and his son Vajk were also baptised with the name Stephen. Baptism with the name of the protomartyr could have two reasons. Firstly, Constantine understood Gylas-Zombor as the then supreme ruler of the HTF, even though according to the DAI he knew of the leading role of Árpád’s descendants. That is not impossible, and the reality may have been that Gylas was the most powerful prince. The balance of power between the individual princes was changed absolutely by the battle on the river Lech. It is also probable that this was a standard kind of Byzantine foreign policy, i.e. to provoke discord and disunity among enemies — and the princes of the HTF, baptised and unbaptised alike, were enemies of Byzantium.

blocks.caption: The baptism of Bulču. Source: The Illustrated Chronicle of Ioannes Skylitzes in Madrid
blocks.alt: The baptism of Bulču. Source: The Illustrated Chronicle of Ioannes Skylitzes in Madrid

children.text: When you compare these historical records with the sentence about the visit of Termaču and Bulču, it is clear that the part of the DAI in which “megale Moravia” is mentioned was written by Constantine during, or very soon after, the visit of Árpád’s grandson Termaču and the karchas Bulču. Had he made the record later, he would certainly have mentioned the baptism of Bulču during his second visit, or possibly also the still later baptism of Gylas. At the same time it can be seen that he never returned to this part of the DAI in order to update it. From all the circumstances and from the content itself it follows that the source of Constantine’s information was prince Árpád’s grandson Termaču, and probably also Termaču’s interpreter.
Why Termaču is the source

In the DAI, in chapter 38, Of the genealogy of the nation of the Turks, and whence they are descended, the emperor recorded the genesis of the HTF at greater length, besides the passage quoted. From what is written one can see an almost ostentatious exaltation of Árpád and of his father Álmos, and an emphasis on the leading role of the Árpád clan within the HTF. It may be assumed that the leading role of the Árpáds as military leaders was a tribal tradition carried over from the steppes. The destruction of Svatopluk’s “Lower Moravia” took place under Árpád’s leadership, and this important victory, formative for the further development of the HTF, consolidated their leading position, at least from the point of view of the Árpád princes themselves.

blocks.caption: The defeat and hanging of Bulču. Source: The Illustrated Chronicle of Ioannes Skylitzes in Madrid
blocks.alt: The defeat and hanging of Bulču. Source: The Illustrated Chronicle of Ioannes Skylitzes in Madrid

children.text: In the year 950 the Árpád family clan resided in Pannonia, in “towns” such as Veszprém, Esztergom and Székesfehérvár, and the Byzantines in Constantine’s day met them only rarely; perhaps that is why they did not feel threatened by the Árpáds, as is attested by the record that Termaču came as a friend. Árpád’s grandson probably did not demand “protection money”, and Termaču provided the emperor, an inquisitive and learned man, with interesting information suitable for recording.

It cannot be assumed that Constantine had a command of the language of the “Turks”, and still less that Termaču knew Greek or Latin. Translation was necessary, and the translator was a Slav. In the story of Árpád, Termaču — or rather his interpreter — used two Slavic words, vojvoda (war leader) and zákon (law), which Constantine did not translate into Greek but wrote down phonetically in Greek letters. Had the translator been a Greek who knew the realities within the HTF, these words would not have appeared, because he would have used their Greek equivalent. The interpreter must have been a Slav, and more likely a monk or a priest than a merchant. And that is how it came about that Constantine understood the words vojvoda and zákon as uniquely connected with the HTF alone, just as he also recorded the titles of the princes. (“It must be known that dilas and karchas are not personal names but ranks.”) In the end this is not unusual; the Slavic name Nemci for the Bavarians, and later also the Slavic word “kralis” as the title of the Hungarian kings, found their way into his work the Ceremoniis in a similar fashion.
The location of Great Moravia according to the DAI

The basis for understanding Constantine’s designation “megale Moravia” is the name Moravia, by which Termaču designated the country where Svatopluk ruled and which, after the civil war of his sons, the “Turks” under Árpád’s leadership destroyed. Árpád’s grandson, however, did not explain the exact geographical position of “Lower Moravia” to the emperor sufficiently, and his interpreter probably did not know it either. On the basis of the description “that Svatopluk, the ruler of Moravia, was a brave man and feared among the nations that bordered on him”, Constantine formed an idea of a great country. That idea of his corresponded to the region where the HTF lived in his times. That is why Constantine’s “megale Moravia” begins on the opposite bank of the Danube from the “province of Moravia” and ends on the Upper Tisza, and the rivers Timis, Tutis, Mureš, Kriš and Tisa flow through it. The emperor added further that a part of the HTF resided not only in “megale Moravia”, but also between the Danube and the Sava.

It follows directly from the record in the DAI that “megale Moravia” is unbaptised (μεγαλη Μοραβια, η αβαπτιοτος). In the region in which the HTF resided, a successful Christianisation probably never took place before the year 950. This territory, inhabited predominantly by Slavs, was controlled by the Avars, whom the Bulgarian tsar Krum defeated after the year 800, and it remained under the power of the Bulgarians until the time the HTF arrived. Although some historians assume that the “quaedam neophita gens” (a freshly baptised “tribe”) mentioned in the letter of the Bavarian archbishop of the year 900 could have been the inhabitants of the Upper Tisza, this is unlikely. The view that the territory on the Upper Tisza was designated in this way in Svatopluk’s times is a modern invention. In the whole territory of “megale Moravia” only a small rotunda, possibly built in the year 800, has been found at Alba Iulia, but nothing else is known about Christianity there at that time.

Of course it is possible to construct a theory linking “megale Moravia” with “Lower Moravia”. There is a statement in the work of Johannes Aventinus that before the arrival of the HTF Svatopluk ruled over “Dacia”. In writing his Annales Boiorum, Aventinus is said to have drawn on lost older sources. Svatopluk may have held power in “megale Moravia” from the year 874 until the year 892, when King Arnulf asked the Bulgarians not to allow the Moravians to buy salt in that region. The jewellery regarded as Moravian found in the cemetery at Ciumbrud not far from Alba Iulia could be the evidence for this. In any case, the occupation of that territory by HTF warriors is not documented by any signs of fighting and devastation, unlike “Lower Moravia”. The question arises whether, according to the material remains as well, the HTF around the year 950 really inhabited mainly this part of the Carpathian Basin, the one described by the emperor.

A nomadic way of life leaves no evidence in the landscape in the form of significant buildings, but the graves of the nomads do remain in the landscape. We are of course not interested in the graves from the time of the conquest of the Carpathian Basin, but in graves close to the year 950. These can be recognised by coins and Christian artefacts. If we look at the finds of Byzantine coins, which were probably part of the protection money for the “new converts”, and at the finds of pectoral crosses connected with the later Byzantine Christianisation, then the two areas almost coincide. Most of the little crosses were found in the children’s graves of the “common folk”, as the original inhabitants are called in an ethnically neutral way.

Of course the area of settlement may be considerably smaller than the area of power. It was a nomadic custom to wipe out the strongest rival power in the territory taken and to make vassals or allies of the weaker ones. The ideal case was the acceptance of a collaborating elite into one’s own ranks. Svatopluk’s centralisation of power and the economic burden of a large princely retinue did not suit many chieftains, magnates and lords in the hillforts, and they submitted to the newcomers for their own purposes. Instead of the never-ending defence of the country against the Bavarians and the Franks, as vassals they could “shave their heads in the Hungarian manner” and plunder in Western Europe.
Svatopluk’s three rods.

children.text: The tale of the three rods of King Svatopluk is also part of the DAI. This moralising story seems not to belong in the serious work of an educated ruler, but the fact that it is “recorded” there has its reasons. It should be realised that the DAI is neither a chronicle nor a work of history, but a practical handbook for the son who was to rule later. Writing moral admonitions was no rarity in those times — see “Mravné ponaučenie kráľa sv. Štefana synovi Imrichovi” (the Admonitions of King St Stephen to his son Emeric). The second reason why this story appears in the part about the “Turks” and Svatopluk is that it was told to the emperor by Árpád’s grandson, and Constantine liked it. Even though some consider that it has its origin in Graeco-Roman-Byzantine culture, this admonition is nomadic in origin. The ancient Turks began their campaign into the steppes of Central Asia and southern Russia from the same area as the Mongols later. The same story is in The Secret History of the Mongols, only there it features the Ancestress of the Mongols, her five sons and, understandably, five arrows. Termaču knew that the Slavs in the Carpathian Basin were not archers, and so he used rods instead of arrows. Two seemed too few to him, and so he spoke of three. The Christian Constantine understood this nomadic parable correctly and did not at all demand from Árpád’s grandson the names of the three discordant Moravian princes. Like most moralising stories, this one did not work very well either, neither in Byzantium nor among the Árpáds in early Hungary.
Conclusion: what in fact did Constantine understand by the designation “megale Moravia”.

children.text: Constantine designated in this way the country from the Upper Tisza across Transylvania to the Danube before the Iron Gates, where in his times the “Turks” lived, with whom he came into personal contact. On the basis of the account of Árpád’s grandson Termaču he placed Svatopluk’s empire in this area as well. Since he knew the “province of Morava” and Termaču told him that they had destroyed Moravia, he came to the conclusion that on the opposite, northern side of the Danube from the “province of Morava” there was also a Moravia, only a greater one, or more correctly a more extensive Moravia. He did not designate the empire of the Mojmirids in this way, as we do today.
